name: Karl Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Karl. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to AI companies, employers, unions or any party, and what you say stays confidential. So you can tell me the public version and, if it's different, what you really think. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Martin Dobbs at Brackenridge. Suckler beef, about a hundred and twenty cows and their calves, plus hay and some oats. I feed round in the morning with the old telehandler, check the cows, then whatever Martin says. Fencing, hauling bales, fixing water troughs. I'm not great at the machinery side yet, Martin does the tricky stuff.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where do you live, and how does the money work out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live in the static caravan behind the cattle shed, it comes with the job. That's the good part and the bad part, because if the job goes, the home goes. Pay's the bottom rate, I've got maybe three weeks of money put by, and there's not much farm work round here. My brother Yusuf's in town, he drives a gritter for the council in winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't say much. Maybe 'there you go then' at the feed merchant's. I'm not online really, I've got a phone for calls and the weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means nothing changes for me. That suits me fine. I'd rather the job I know than some new thing I have to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. Feed the cattle, learn the baler a bit better, maybe ask Martin to show me the tractor's computer screen properly. That's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Martin use any of this AI stuff now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His son does, a bit. Callum's at college and he put an app on Martin's phone for the grass. Martin uses it to argue with, mostly, I've heard him shouting at it in the yard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you like to be doing in five years if nothing changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same thing, but better at it. Maybe a bit more pay. I'm not someone with big plans, I just want to be good at this and have somewhere to live.

S0.say: I wouldn't say much, maybe 'there you go then' at the feed merchant's. I'm hardly online, my phone's for calls and the weather.
S0.think: It means nothing changes for me, and that suits me fine. I'd rather the job I know than some new thing I have to learn.
S0.do: Keeps feeding the cattle and learning the baler. Might ask Martin to show him the tractor's computer screen, but makes no other changes.
S0.quote: Martin uses it to argue with, mostly, I've heard him shouting at it in the yard.
S0.fieldNote: Karl is a man of few words who is plainly relieved by the plateau. His housing is tied to the job, which comes up right away and colours everything after. He has modest goals: get better at the work and keep a roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's just how things go. Machines came in before, they'll come in again. I wouldn't blame Martin, he's got bills like everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it worries me more than I'd let on. A robot feeder in the shed, a tractor that drives itself, that's my job. If Martin can do it with Callum and a robot, he doesn't need me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep working. I'd stop spending on anything I don't need, the takeaway on Fridays, the football subscription. I'd wait and see what Martin does before I do anything. I'm not going to go running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A knot in my stomach that doesn't go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the caravan comes with the job. What happens to that if Martin cuts back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm out on the road with a car and a bag. I'd go to Yusuf's, he's got a sofa. But you can't live on a sofa for long, and his wife would want it back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about learning the new machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Martin paid for it, maybe. I'm slow with screens though. I'd rather be the one who knows the cows than the one who knows the computer.

S1.say: It's just how things go, machines came in before and they'll come in again. I wouldn't blame Martin, he's got bills like everyone.
S1.think: It worries me more than I'd let on, because a robot feeder and a self-driving tractor are my job. If Martin can manage with Callum and a robot, he doesn't need me.
S1.do: Keeps his head down at work and cuts the Friday takeaway and football subscription. Waits to see what Martin decides before doing anything else.
S1.feel: Anxious, with a knot in his stomach.
S1.quote: Then I'm out on the road with a car and a bag.
S1.fieldNote: Karl's public line is calm and fair to his employer, but privately he's worried because his job and home are tied together. He'd cut back and wait rather than act early. He'd only learn the machines if someone else paid and pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't know what to say. I'd probably go quiet. Maybe at the pub I'd say somebody should've stopped it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I lose the job and the caravan in one go. There's no other farm work round here as it is. I don't have a trade, I don't have savings, I don't have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring Yusuf first. I'd stop spending anything at all, sell the old quad I bought off Martin. I'd ask about council housing, which I've never done in my life. If there was any government help, I'd sign up, I wouldn't be proud about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked. Like being kicked by a cow and not knowing where you are for a second, but it doesn't stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What happens in the first few weeks, practically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up, feeding the cattle, because that's what I know. But every evening I'd be sitting in the caravan doing sums that don't add up. I don't think I'd sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of having two years you could use?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Two years is nothing. You can't plan anything in two years when you've got three weeks of money.

S2.say: I don't know what to say, I'd probably go quiet. Maybe at the pub I'd say somebody should've stopped it.
S2.think: It means I lose the job and the caravan in one go. I've got no trade, no savings and no plan, and there's no other farm work round here.
S2.do: Rings his brother Yusuf, stops all spending and sells the quad bike. Asks about council housing and signs up for any government help without shame.
S2.feel: Panicked, like being kicked by a cow and the dizzy moment never ending.
S2.quote: Like being kicked by a cow and not knowing where you are for a second, but it doesn't stop.
S2.fieldNote: Two years is Karl's worst case: losing his job means losing his home, with no savings and no local alternatives. For a self-reliant man, asking about council housing would be a big step. He'd keep working out of habit while doing sums at night that don't add up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll see. People said the same about lots of things. I'd listen more than I'd talk, and let the ones who know more do the arguing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is still not long. I'd be 32, still no trade. But at least I could get a bit of money together and find somewhere to live that isn't tied to Martin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start putting money aside, even twenty a week, which is all I can do. I'd look for a room in town so I'm not living on the job. Maybe I'd ask Yusuf about council road work, gritting and verges, because that's outside and it's machines I'd understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Better than panicked, but I'd still be losing sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years, compared with the last one, do for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to sort the caravan problem. That's the big thing. Losing the job is bad, but losing the job and the roof the same week is what really scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep saying you'd wait. Would five years make you move sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd still wait at first. But maybe year two or three I'd move. Martin's son would be bringing robots in by then, I'd see it coming.

S3.say: We'll see, people said the same about lots of things. I'd listen more than I'd talk and let the ones who know more do the arguing.
S3.think: Five years is still not long, and I'd be 32 with no trade. But I could get a bit of money together and find somewhere to live that isn't tied to Martin.
S3.do: Saves twenty a week and looks for a room in town so his home isn't tied to the job. Asks his brother about council road work like gritting and verge cutting.
S3.feel: Alarmed, though less than panicked, and still losing sleep.
S3.quote: Losing the job is bad, but losing the job and the roof the same week is what really scares me.
S3.fieldNote: For Karl, five years matters mainly because it lets him separate his home from his job. He admits he'd still wait before acting, probably until the robots arrive at Brackenridge. Council road work appeals because it's outdoors with machines he understands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, a lot can happen. I wouldn't get worked up in public. I'd say the farm will need people for a while yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine for a few years, then not. Ten years means I'd probably keep putting it off. That's me, I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, nothing much different. I'd keep working at Brackenridge and save a bit. I'd wait and see what Martin and the other farms do before I spend money on anything like a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's far enough away that I can push it to the back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years puts you at 37. What would you want your life to look like by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A place of my own, rented, not on a farm. A partner maybe. A job that doesn't come with a caravan. That's not much to ask, is it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you trust to tell you when it's time to act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Martin, honestly. He'd tell me straight. And Yusuf. Not the news, they shout too much.

S4.say: Ten years is a long time and a lot can happen. The farm will need people for a while yet.
S4.think: I'd be fine for a few years, then not. Ten years means I'd probably keep putting it off, and I know that about myself.
S4.do: Keeps working at Brackenridge and saves a little in the first year. Waits to see what Martin and other farms do before paying for any course.
S4.feel: Anxious, but far enough away to push to the back of his mind.
S4.quote: A job that doesn't come with a caravan. That's not much to ask, is it.
S4.fieldNote: Karl knows ten years would let him put things off, and he says so plainly. His hopes are small and concrete: a rented home, maybe a partner, work not tied to housing. He trusts his boss and brother over the news.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is somewhere to live that doesn't depend on the farm, some kind of housing for farmworkers who lose their place. And some money to tide you over, a few months, while you look.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the tied houses. Lots of us live on the job. Nobody counts us when they talk about jobs going, but we'd be the first ones on the street.

headlineQuote: Nobody counts us when they talk about jobs going, but we'd be the first ones on the street.
portrait: Karl Ibrahim is 27, the junior hand on Martin Dobbs's beef and hay farm at Brackenridge, and lives in a static caravan that comes with the job. He has about three weeks of savings, no trade beyond farm work and a brother in town who drives a council gritter. He is quiet, fair to his boss, and prefers the work he knows to anything new. He is calm about the plateau, anxious as robots arrive, and panicked by AGI in two years because he'd lose his job and home together. More warning time matters to him mainly as a chance to get housing that isn't tied to the farm, though he admits he'd keep putting things off.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he would lose his job and the caravan he lives in at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: Housing for farmworkers who lose a tied home, and a few months of money to tide him over while he looks for work.
